after: ## The civil courts at first instance
alt: The County Court, one national court at many hearing centres, hears most civil claims before district and circuit judges. The High Court has three divisions: King’s Bench (higher-value contract and tort, Commercial Court), Chancery (business, property, trusts, insolvency, probate) and Family. A money claim normally starts in the High Court only if worth more than £100,000, or £50,000 for personal injury.
caption: Most claims start in the County Court; only high-value claims start in the High Court.

after: ## A claim from start to finish
alt: Six numbered stages of a civil claim: pre-action conduct under a protocol, issuing a claim form, the defendant’s response, allocation to a track, case management and trial, and enforcement. The Civil Procedure Rules 1998 aim to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost.
caption: Settlement is expected before issue; a defended claim is then allocated to a track.

alt: Four tracks along a value scale: small claims up to £10,000 (informal, costs generally not recoverable), fast track £10,000 to £25,000 (one-day trial), intermediate track £25,000 to £100,000 from October 2023 (up to three days) and multi-track over £100,000 or complex. Small claims limits are lower for personal injury, road traffic injury and housing disrepair. Complexity, parties, oral evidence, wider importance and the parties’ views also matter.
caption: Value sets the normal track, but complexity can push a claim higher.

alt: An appeal ladder: district judge to circuit judge, circuit judge to High Court judge, High Court to Court of Appeal (Civil Division), Court of Appeal to Supreme Court on a point of law of general public importance. A leapfrog route goes from the High Court straight to the Supreme Court. Appeals need permission and succeed only if the decision was wrong or unjust through serious procedural irregularity; second appeals need an important point of principle or practice or another compelling reason.
caption: Each appeal goes one level up, with permission, and is not a rehearing.

alt: The First-tier Tribunal hears cases at first instance in chambers such as Social Entitlement, Immigration and Asylum, Tax and Property. Appeals on points of law go to the Upper Tribunal (Administrative Appeals, Immigration and Asylum, Tax and Chancery, Lands), then with permission to the Court of Appeal. Employment Tribunals and the Employment Appeal Tribunal sit outside the two tiers, with ACAS early conciliation first.
caption: Two tiers of chambers, then the Court of Appeal; employment sits alongside.

alt: A timeline of court attitudes to mediation: Dunnett v Railtrack (2002), a winner denied costs for refusing to consider mediation; Halsey (2004), courts cannot compel mediation but can penalise unreasonable refusal; Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil (2023), courts can order non-court dispute resolution if fair and proportionate. Below: uses, strengths and weaknesses of mediation.
caption: Courts moved from encouraging mediation to being able to order it.

alt: Three methods on a scale of control. In negotiation the parties or their lawyers agree a settlement themselves; in mediation a neutral mediator helps them reach their own agreement, binding only if made a contract or court order; a tribunal or court imposes a binding decision. Part 36 offers encourage negotiated settlement by penalising a party who rejects an offer and does no better at trial.
caption: The more neutral help is added, the less control the parties keep.

after: ## Worked example: advising on a forum
alt: Kim’s route in six steps: negotiate with a letter before claim; follow pre-action conduct; issue in the County Court on the small claims track as the claim is under £10,000; the court’s free mediation service; a small claims hearing before a district judge; and an appeal only with permission to a circuit judge.
caption: Negotiate, mediate, then the small claims track: the right forum for £6,500.
